clinicalPearls: Acquired hypermelanosis that develops at sites of previous inflammation or injury (acne, eczema, lichen planus, trauma, procedures) and mirrors the distribution of the preceding dermatosis
Far more frequent, more intense and more persistent in darker skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick IV-VI)
Wood-lamp examination distinguishes epidermal pigment, which is accentuated and brown, from dermal pigment, which appears blue-grey and is not accentuated, and this guides treatment expectations
Epidermal pigment responds reasonably to photoprotection and topical lightening agents, whereas dermal pigment is far more refractory and slow to clear
Interface dermatoses such as lichen planus cause basal damage and pigment incontinence, producing prominent, long-lasting dermal pigmentation
Management rests on treating the underlying inflammatory dermatosis, strict photoprotection and topical depigmenting agents, with chemical peels or laser as cautious adjuncts
Overly aggressive treatment, peels or lasers can paradoxically worsen pigmentation, particularly in darker skin
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous inflammation stimulates melanocytes to increase melanin synthesis through inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes and cytokines, producing epidermal hypermelanosis. When the inflammation damages the basal layer and dermoepidermal junction, melanin is released and drops into the dermis (pigment incontinence), where it is engulfed by melanophages to give a deeper, longer-lasting dermal hyperpigmentation. The depth of pigment therefore reflects the intensity and level of the preceding inflammatory process.
additionalDifferentials: Solar lentigines and other benign lentigines
Residual fixed drug eruption or other drug-induced pigmentation
Ashy dermatosis and lichen planus pigmentosus
additionalInvestigations: Wood-lamp examination to gauge epidermal versus dermal pigment
Dermoscopy to assess pigment pattern and depth
Review of medication history and the triggering dermatosis
Patch testing where a contact or photocontact cause is suspected
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis or an alternative pigmented lesion is uncertain
redFlags: An irregular, changing or atypical pigmented lesion that could represent melanoma rather than benign pigmentation
Ongoing or poorly controlled underlying inflammatory dermatosis driving continued pigmentation
Signs of exogenous ochronosis from prolonged misuse of topical lightening agents
Widespread pigmentation suggesting a systemic or drug-related cause
reference.prognosis: Epidermal post-inflammatory pigment usually fades gradually over months once the inflammation is controlled, whereas dermal pigment may persist for years or be effectively permanent; darker skin phototypes tend to have slower resolution.
pitfalls: Failing to treat the underlying inflammatory dermatosis, so pigmentation recurs
Using aggressive lasers or peels that worsen pigmentation, especially in darker skin
Mislabelling melasma or another primary pigmentary disorder as post-inflammatory change
Neglecting photoprotection, which allows sun exposure to deepen and prolong the pigmentation
